I think we'll naturally develop intuition and infrastructure for fault-tolerant ways to implement LLMs in non-verifiable domains, i.e. requiring multiple, independent agents agree on a direction from multiple angles before taking an action.

But we're definitely very early on this trend.

You're missing the biggest suggestion from the GP's post: that the key to LLM success is verifiability.

Software has high verifiability through compilers, linters, static analysis, leak/memory corruption detection tools, or the very least, running the program to see if it crashes.

Math (as has been making the headlines recently) has high verifiability through automated theorem provers. Notably some of the non-mechanized math results from LLMs have been demonstrated to be wrong (and presumably many more are being checked; these aren't exactly easy to understand proofs).

Game playing (chess, go, Star Craft, etc.) is similarly verifiable: you get your score and you always know how you did in the end (even if not in the moment).

Making assumptions about LLMs in non-veriable domains is making a claim about LLMs that doesn't match their current capabilities. Maybe they'll get there and maybe they won't; I can speculate as well as you can but we're both guessing, so I'm not sure how much value the speculation has.

I think LLM's will prove to be useful in any domain where most work happens in front of a computer. As LLM's make programming cheap, they also reduce the cost of building new software that automates work currently performed by humans in other fields.

If you provide best models with all the data and context an average white collar worker has to perform their job, in most cases they will do just fine. I think this is misreading the data.

We are functionally in a recession. The only way this isn't true is because of AI investment [1]. Additionally, GDP itself is flawed because it is propped up by housing, specifically imputed rent [2]. Another ticking time bomb is the $4T private equity backlog [3].

The real product of AI of labor displacement and wage suppression.

We're not producing anything anymore. All we're doing is driving up revenues on inelastic demand on things like food, housing, electricity and health care. That's all PE is. And that's all our economy does now.

I really think people are underestimating just how close to breaking point our society is.

I have worked in multiple companies where the internally developed software was central to the business success, yet it was handled in an extremely bad way, preventing it from using even a small percentage of its potential.

The management did constantly override technical decisions and/or switched the main goals/vison around all the time, preventing the development from finishing anything.

It's been almost five years since I left there, and I still have several friends in that company. One of them is one of the users of the software, another one is a developer who cares, but he could not switch because he is stuck there for several reasons. One of the main reasons being that he has medical issues that make most companies reject him by default.
They keep me updated about the companies progress, or the lack of it.
The latter guy told me this week, that the company made less progress in the last four years, than it did within a few weeks while the original dev team worked there. And he really wasn't exaggerating. Oh, the company has a big AI budget and they made pretty much every model available to all employees. They just can't use it for good ideas, because they will be garbled up by the management and turned around to be bad. 
As long as they don't replace the management with AI, this technology will not improve their business.
